newsitem.title: USA: Alleged CIA turncoat to seek bail, plead not guilty.
newsitem.headline: Alleged CIA turncoat to seek bail, plead not guilty.

text.p: Harold Nicholson, the Central Intelligence Agency officer charged with conspiracy to commit espionage for Moscow, will plead not guilty and seek pre-trial release from jail, his lawyer said on Wednesday.

"He will plead not guilty," court-appointed attorney Jonathan Shapiro said in a telephone interview with Reuters. He added that he would ask the judge at a scheduled pre-trial hearing on Monday to release Nicholson, 46, pending trial.

Shapiro said he would argue for bail or other guarantees the court might seek to ensure that Nicholson, the highest-ranking CIA officer to be charged with spying for Russia, was "not going to flee, which he is not."

A 16-year veteran of the spy agency's covert operations directorate, Nicholson has been held without bail in a city jail in Alexandria, Virginia, a Washington suburb, since he was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation at Dulles Airport on Saturday as he prepared to leave for Switzerland, allegedly to turn over more secrets to his Russian handlers.

The government has accused Nicholson of giving away the identities of undercover CIA officers and informants, along with an unknown quantity of other secrets, for at least the past two years, for at least $120,000 in cash payments.
Prosecutors have said they would oppose bail for fear Nicholson might flee and give away more of his knowledge of some of the most sensitive U.S. intelligence secrets.

Shapiro declined to discuss what advice he was giving Nicholson about cooperating with investigators from the CIA and the FBI who are trying to gauge the damage he allegedly did to U.S. intelligence sources and methods.
He said he planned to stick with the case as long as it lasted. Shapiro, of the Alexandria firm Shapiro & Associates, has 22 years of experience as a criminal defence lawyer.

At Monday's hearing in federal district court, the judge will decide whether the government has shown enough evidence to warrant keeping Nicholson in jail, a likely outcome based on other recent spy cases, including that of Aldrich Ames, who pleaded guilty in 1994 to spying for Moscow for nine years.

U.S. counterspies suspect Nicholson may have compromised a generation of CIA covert operatives he helped school as a trainer from 1994 until four months ago at Camp Peary, the CIA base near Williamsburg, Virginia. Earlier in his career, Nicholson served as CIA station chief in Romania and deputy chief of station in Malaysia.
